extracted.intended_audience: biologists and statisticians studying evolution, genetic selection, and quantitative heredity
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and conducting statistical observations and experiments to detect genetic (reproductive) selection, to measure how fertility correlates with characters, and to quantify forms of inheritance between relatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine correlation of fertility with other characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether fertility is really correlated with any other characters. Is genetic selection a reality?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explicitly lists this as a primary empirical question biologists should answer. Investigations should determine if different magnitudes of character are associated with different grades of fertility; statistical evidence (e.g. comparing class means/medians and distributions) is required rather than verbal argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine how the character of maximum fertility differentiates with type
rubrics_metrics.description: If genetic selection is real, how does a differentiation of the character a of maximum fertility take place, when there is differentiation of type?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a follow-up empirical problem: when types differentiate, does the character associated with maximum fertility also differentiate, and by what mechanism? The author frames this as of 'utmost importance' and requiring targeted investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method to detect genetic selection by reweighting individuals by offspring
rubrics_metrics.description: Take, say, 1000 mated individuals of one sex, find their type; then reckon the same thousand individuals once for each individual offspring of the same sex that they have. If fertility is not a function of the character under investigation the type will not be sensibly changed; if it is, there will be a sensible change of type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as one of the most direct empirical methods to ascertain genetic selection. Implementation guidance: record parental type distribution, then weight parents by their same-sex offspring counts and compare distributions to detect shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sufficiently large samples and amplify preliminary statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Current small-sample statistics (example: 200 wives, 452 daughters) want amplifying at least five-fold to draw stronger inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes that some presented statistics are suggestive but underpowered; recommends substantially larger sample sizes before making firm conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and compare class means, standard deviations, and probable errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use summary statistics (mean stature, standard deviation, probable error) to compare groups (e.g. wives, mothers, daughters) and infer differential fertility effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret small differences in light of probable error; examine directionality and consistency across multiple comparisons rather than relying on single-point differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure fertility by counting/weighting seed or offspring per class/value
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe the frequency distribution of some character (leaves, flowers, seed vessels) and then measure grades of fertility associated with each class by counting/weighing/measuring the seed from the same number of plants or capsules of each class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance and examples given (stigmatic bands in poppy and segmentation in Nigella): fertility concentrated near modal classes; extremes often relatively or absolutely sterile. Repeat across species and larger scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical prediction: type will change toward character of maximum fertility
rubrics_metrics.description: If fertility be correlated with any organ or character, then the organism cannot be stable but must progressively change until the type becomes identical with the character or organ associated with maximum fertility, and until variability becomes that of the offspring of the type only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a testable theoretical consequence: expect progressive change of modal value and reduction of variability (unless opposed by selection mortality). Use longitudinal or generational data to test convergence of modal value toward maximal-fertility character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish net vs gross fertility in analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between net and gross fertility is important (e.g., working classes have greater gross but less individual net fertility than professional classes; marriage rates affect total net fertility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For evolutionary and social/economic analyses, focus on net fertility where relevant; be aware that gross fertility alone can mislead when comparing classes or populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses/framework for origin of species incorporating genetic selection
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Differentiation of type owing to change of environment (natural selection). (b) Maintenance of difference of type owing to some barrier to inter-breeding (sexual selection). (c) Check to prevent reproductive selection destroying the differentiation, either (i) a stringent periodic selection, or (ii) a differentiation of the most fertile character associated with differentiation of type. (d) Progressive change of types until mechanical or physiological mutual sterility arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author presents these as stages that can be statistically investigated. Each stage represents a testable claim or mechanism to be examined empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical investigation preferred over verbal discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Such investigation and not verbal discussion can alone throw light on the problem of evolution; every stage can be statistically investigated by experiment or observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments or observational studies to address each hypothesized stage; quantify distributions, fertility associations, and selection effects rather than relying on qualitative argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify forms of inheritance and study each statistically
rubrics_metrics.description: Three chief forms of inheritance: (a) Blended Inheritance; (b) Exclusive Inheritance; (c) Particulate Inheritance. All three require careful statistical study, though little has been done except for blended inheritance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistical data from relatives and gametic analyses to distinguish blending, exclusivity/prepotency, and particulate patterns (examples: coat-colour blending vs piebald horses; eye-colour mostly exclusive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative linear model of heredity from gamete deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Model the individual's deviation s as s = a1 x1 + a2 x2 + ... + b1 y1 + b2 y2 + ... where x's are deviations in a spermatozoon and y's in an ovum; the a's define inheritance from the male, the b's from the female. If both contribute, inheritance is blended; if one set dominates, that element is prepotent; if coefficients are sensibly zero for one parent, inheritance is exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a quantitative framework: estimate coefficients from data on many characters and relatives. Use the model to interpret blended vs prepotent vs exclusive inheritance and to predict offspring distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate environmental influence on gamete characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the gamete deviations purely determined by bathmic (internal) influences, or are they related to environment? Does growth and nourishment of the individual influence reproductive organs and thereby the characters of gametes produced under different circumstances?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author urges hesitation before assuming gametes unaffected by environment; study correlations between reproductive and other organs and test gamete character variation across controlled environmental differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate sexual selection among gametes (assortative/pangamic processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there any form of sexual selection among the gametes themselves? A spermatozoon with definite characters may have more chance than its fellows to conjugate with particular ova — i.e., preferential or assortative mating may exist among gametes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments/observations to detect non-random gamete conjugation, especially when many gametes are available; consider how mixing diverse gamete groups might permit extreme gametic deviations to conjugate and produce large divergences in zygotes (explaining some atavism or hybrid phenomena).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate telegony claims with quantitative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Does previous sexual union of a female influence the characters of subsequently produced ova (telegony)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author reports no quantitative evidence in man and cites Ewart's experiment repeating the quagga case attributing subsequent markings to reversion rather than telegony. Recommend careful experimental replication and quantitative analysis before accepting telegony claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure heredity by correlations among many relative pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A and B be a pair of relatives. Measure the same organ in many pairs (e.g., 1000 pairs) and form a correlation table for the organs of A,B pairs to investigate direct and cross heredity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author illustrates with father-son stature example: fathers of a given height have sons forming an array whose mean is nearer the population mean (regression to the mean). Use correlation/regression analysis on large samples to quantify heredity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for variability at individual and race levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Offspring of self-fertilisation and parthenogenetic reproduction form an array of variability/standard-deviation with a mode usually divergent from the parent's value; there is variability among parts of the same individual and among offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitatively describe variabilities (individual type vs race type). Recognize that variability among brethren follows mathematically from within-individual variability of 'undifferentiated like organs'. Use these distributions when modelling inheritance and expected offspring variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat and extend species-specific observations before generalizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations on fertility-character associations (e.g., poppy and nigella capsule fertility) require repetition on a wider number of species and on a larger scale before general conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's empirical examples are preliminary; experimental replication, cross-species sampling, and larger-scale studies are needed to substantiate proposed laws (e.g., fertility concentrated at modal types).
